8.0.s.en: (1) The plague of frogs (the second plague)

8.0.0.en: God commanded Moses to go into Pharaoh's palace and order him to let the children of Israel go, otherwise God would strike him with the frogs, which were sacred to the god Osiris. So God turned what they considered sacred into a cause of great distress for them, that they might feel the weakness and futility of their gods. From another angle, the Egyptian priests were careful about their washing and purity, and some of them considered frogs unclean and a defilement of their purity; so the frogs' attack upon them in this plague declared their inability to purify themselves.

8.1.0.en: Ovens: the plural of oven, that is, a furnace in which bread is baked.

8.1.1.en: Kneadingtroughs: large earthenware vessels in which a little water and leaven are mixed in preparation for turning it into bread.

8.1.2.en: Moses threatened Pharaoh that the frogs would come out of the river and its surroundings and attack the houses of the Egyptians, in their bedchambers, their places for kneading dough and their baking ovens, and would trouble them with their noise and foul smell.

8.1.3.en: The frogs signify the sins that make much noise but are of no benefit, such as the lusts of pride and the love of display. Let us look at the end of what we do or say, however brilliant it may seem: does it give us peace and growth in our relationship with God, or not?

8.2.0.en: Ponds: the plural of pond, which is a gathering of water, that is, a pool of fresh water.

8.2.1.en: Pharaoh was not moved by the divine threat, so Aaron struck the River Nile with his rod, and the frogs came up from the river, the streams and the pools, and spread into all the houses of the Egyptians and troubled them greatly with their noise and smell.

8.3.0.en: Pharaoh persisted in his evil and ordered the magicians to imitate this plague, so they brought up frogs from the river. This was a satanic work, yet they were unable to stop the plague, for Satan produces evil but cannot rescue his followers. As for God, He struck them with the frogs to discipline them and to show the weakness of their gods, so that they might hate their false sacred objects.

8.3.1.en: Do not be dazzled by evil, but seek what is good and everything that gives you peace, for the works of God are always for the edification and peace of man, while the works of Satan are always for destruction and for disturbing people.

8.4.0.en: Pharaoh and all the Egyptians were distressed by the frogs and his helplessness was exposed, so he begged Moses to pray to his God to take the frogs away from him, after his magicians had been unable to remove them. This was not faith in God, but he knew that God was stronger than his gods.

8.4.1.en: If you know the truth, do not resist it or argue, but submit, even if your weakness shows, because your arguing reveals your weakness more than before.

8.5.0.en: Moses agreed to Pharaoh's request, and in order to show the power of God, who is able to do all things, he asked Pharaoh to set the time for their removal so that God would remove them and Pharaoh would believe in His power. Pharaoh asked for them to be removed quickly, that is, on the very next day, and Moses agreed.

8.6.0.en: Moses prayed to God, and the frogs that had spread through the land of Egypt died, and remained only in the river. They gathered them from the houses and the fields into heaps, and the whole of Egypt gave off a very foul stench. This shows the force of the plague and makes them hate their great god Osiris, whose sacred objects, the frogs, had become a cause of great distress for them.

8.6.1.en: Pagan worship appears great to those who cling to it, like the lusts that appear alluring and pleasant but leave behind only distress and degradation, just as the frogs turned into stinking heaps. So do not slip after lusts, however great their allure, for they are all temporary and passing; flee from them and keep away from everything that encourages them, so that you may keep yourself pure and in peace.

8.7.0.en: After the plague was lifted, Pharaoh returned to his hardness and refused to let the children of Israel go.

8.7.1.en: Do not take lightly God's longsuffering by deceiving Him and going back on your promises, for you will lose His mercies.

8.8.s.en: (2) The plague of lice (the third plague)

8.8.0.en: This time Moses did not threaten Pharaoh but struck the plague as God commanded. He struck the dust spread over all the land of Egypt, and when the wind lifted it and it became dust in the air, this dust turned into a great multitude of lice that bit the Egyptians and the beasts. They were greatly troubled, and in addition the priests, who were famous for cleanliness and frequent washing, were defiled by the frogs and then by the bites of the lice, which they also considered uncleanness, and their gods did not protect them from it, so their helplessness was shown. Thus the purpose of this plague appears, which is:

8.8.1.en: (1) God troubled them with a small insect so that they might repent, rather than with beasts that would kill them and destroy them.

8.8.2.en: (2) That they could be troubled with small insects, with no need for great beasts.

8.8.3.en: (3) The loss of the outward cleanliness they cared about, that perhaps they might pay attention to the filth of their hearts, soiled by sin, and repent.

8.8.4.en: The bites of the lice signify gentle, deceptive words and thoughts, or sinful pleasures that appear kind and gentle but leave behind pain and suffering within man.

8.9.0.en: Pharaoh commanded his magicians to remove the plague of lice from him, but they were unable, and they themselves were under it, so they declared that this plague was from God, who is stronger than all their gods. But Pharaoh was enraged at his helplessness and hardened his heart. Here God shows the weakness of Satan and his pagan gods before the power of God, that perhaps the Egyptians might understand and believe in God.

8.9.1.en: Do not reject the word of God on the tongue of those around you, for it is a message calling you to repentance, whether these people are your friends, strangers to you, or even those who wrong you, because God is the One who leads your life and arranges all your affairs, and He always seeks you to return to Him.

8.10.s.en: (3) The plague of flies (the fourth plague)

8.10.0.en: Swarms of flies: either the well-known insect, the fly, of which there are many kinds, some of them large and troubling and frightening to many; or a kind of scarab, which is a small black insect resembling a beetle, that walks on the ground, ugly in appearance, and which the Egyptians worshipped.

8.10.1.en: God commanded Moses to meet Pharaoh, who had gone out either for a festival at the River Nile or for a walk, and to order him to let God's people go, and to threaten him that if he did not, God would strike him with swarms of flies that would spread through all the land of Egypt. The plague of flies shows the inability of the Egyptian gods to protect their followers if they could not lift this plague from them; and if the scarab is what is meant, then this plague turns their objects of worship into a cause of distress for them.

8.11.0.en: In this verse God shows what happens in all the plagues, namely that they did not fall upon the children of Israel, to show the power of God, which protects His children and disciplines the wicked, that perhaps they might repent. Moses also set the time of this plague for the next day, which shows the power of God, who sets times and does what He says.

8.12.0.en: The flies spread through all the land of Egypt, troubled the people and halted work, until the land of Egypt was ruined because everything in it came to a standstill, through the spoiling of food and plants, the agitation of the animals and the distress of man.

8.13.0.en: The abomination of the Egyptians: the Egyptians worshipped some cattle, such as the calf, and if it was slaughtered before them they would be enraged and consider this slaughter an evil and strange act, indeed an insult and a defilement of their objects of worship, that is, an abomination.

8.13.1.en: Because of the severity of the plagues, Pharaoh tried to find a solution for the children of Israel, which was that they should sacrifice to their God in the land of Goshen in which they lived. Moses refused, because the Egyptians worship sheep and cattle, and if they sacrificed them before them, the Egyptians would be enraged against them and kill them.

8.14.0.en: Because of the severity of the trial, Pharaoh agreed to the children of Israel leaving Egypt as Moses had told him, but on condition that they not go very far. He did not agree to their going a three days' journey away, since Moses wanted separation from Egypt and its pagan worship, so that they might spend the rest of their days worshipping God, while Pharaoh asked that they not go far from Egypt so that he could control them and exploit them in building cities and in farming. It is noticeable that Pharaoh had begun to feel the power of the God of Moses and Aaron, so he asked them to pray for him before their God, who is stronger than the gods of the Egyptians.

8.15.1.en: Moses agreed to pray that God would lift the fourth plague, and in faith he set the time of its removal, which was the next day, but he warned Pharaoh against going back on his promise, because that is falsehood and deceit that exposes him to God's punishment.

8.15.2.en: Do not take lightly lying or any sin, because it is directed against God Himself, and the wages of sin is death.

8.16.0.en: Moses prayed, and God removed the plague completely from all the land of Egypt.

8.17.0.en: Pharaoh returned to the hardness of his heart, went back on his promise and refused to let the children of Israel go. The plagues of the murrain of cattle, the boils, and the hail and fire.

9.0.s.en: (1) The plague of the murrain of cattle (the fifth plague)

9.0.0.en: God commanded Moses to repeat the demand to Pharaoh to let his people go, otherwise He would strike all the cattle of Egypt with murrain and they would die.

9.0.1.en: Some cattle, such as the bull Apis, were sacred and were worshipped by the Egyptians, since the god Osiris was thought to dwell in it, so the death of the cattle shows the weakness of the god Osiris, who is one of the most important of the Egyptian gods. In this plague a divine retribution appears, which is:

9.0.2.en: 1- His protection of the cattle of His people and the death of the cattle of the wicked and stubborn, that is, the Egyptians.

9.0.3.en: 2- The overthrow of the pagan worship that worships animals, such as the bull Apis.

9.0.4.en: 3- The power of God is shown, in which He sets the time and the place, striking the cattle in the field and on the mountain, that is, everywhere the Egyptians own cattle, and the time is tomorrow.

9.0.5.en: 4- God's shattering of the pride of the great and also the strength of the army that uses horses, by their death. The death of the cattle signifies the death of the animal lusts within man, that is, God helps them to leave their lusts so that they may believe in Him.

9.0.6.en: Here God's longsuffering toward the stubborn and the rejecting is shown, that perhaps they might repent, so He repeats His demand that His people be let go and repeats the plagues, that perhaps they might fear Him and repent.

9.1.0.en: God's protection and blessing of His children is shown in the fact that the cattle of the children of Israel did not die.

9.1.1.en: Trust in God's blessing upon you, however much those around you persecute you and trouble you, for He compensates you by blessing what you have and keeping it, and He also grants you peace and joy because you feel that God is with you.

9.2.0.en: God showed His power in setting the time of the plague, so that no one could say that it was due to anything other than God. All the cattle that belonged to the Egyptians died, but of those that belonged to the children of Israel not one died.

9.3.0.en: Pharaoh was alarmed by the death of all his cattle and sent messengers to the land of Goshen to learn what had happened to the numerous cattle of the children of Israel, since they worked as shepherds, and he found all their cattle unharmed. Instead of believing, he became enraged and hardened his heart and refused to let the children of Israel go to worship God.

9.3.1.en: When you see God's blessing with others, look for their virtues and the grace that is with them, so that you may follow their example instead of envying them or being jealous of them.

9.4.s.en: (2) The plague of boils (the sixth plague)

9.4.0.en: This is the sixth plague, in which God commanded Moses to take ashes of the furnace (the oven or the altar on which sacrifices are burned) and throw them into the air, so that they became boils breaking forth with sores, that is, pus, on all the Egyptians, whether the king, the people or the priests, and even the magicians (v. 11). It is painful, and in addition it defiles the priests, who care about their purity when they approach the gods, and it gives an ugly appearance and troublesome signs of disease.

9.4.1.en: In their worship the Egyptians used to offer human sacrifices to their gods, burning them and scattering their ashes, believing that every particle of ash was a blessing from the gods. In this plague Moses showed them the futility of their worship, since this ash became painful boils on their bodies.

9.4.2.en: This plague of boils signifies the sins that disfigure man before God and pain his heart, so that he loses his peace.

9.5.0.en: Moses sprinkled the ashes, and they became boils on the Egyptians and their beasts.

9.5.1.en: One wonders, where did the Egyptians get beasts after the previous plague (the murrain of cattle)? They may have bought cattle from the children of Israel after their own cattle died, or they may have bought them from the surrounding countries such as Sudan and Libya.

9.5.2.en: The boils also appeared on the diviners and magicians who assisted Pharaoh, so the weakness of Pharaoh and his helpers was revealed.

9.5.3.en: It is noticeable that Moses sprinkled the ashes toward heaven to announce that this plague was a heavenly punishment for them, that is, from God and not from their pagan gods. This plague was later called the botch of Egypt, as in (Deut 28:27), and God used to threaten the pagan peoples with it.

9.6.0.en: Pharaoh persisted in his stubbornness and hardness of heart, although this was the sixth plague, and the power of his gods had been shattered before him and his weakness and that of all his helpers had been shown.

9.6.1.en: Would that you would benefit from your weaknesses and repent before the opportunity is lost, for stubbornness shows your ignorance and deprives you of God's mercies.

9.7.s.en: (3) The plague of hail and fire (the seventh plague)

9.7.0.en: God sent a rebuke to Pharaoh with Moses for his stubbornness in not letting His people go, and declared to him that He was able to kill him and all his people, but that He kept him in order to give him an opportunity to repent and to show His wonders through his hardness.

9.8.0.en: He threatened him that He would rain hail, that is, sharp balls or sheets of ice, descending in great quantities from heaven, striking and killing everyone they meet. This plague is very great, so God warned him of it that perhaps he might repent, and kept it near the end because of its severity; it is the seventh plague, which shows the divine wrath against the stubborn and unbelieving, and in it the power of God is shown by setting the time of the plague by the day and the hour, in His saying, "To morrow about this time."

9.9.0.en: God warned Pharaoh and the Egyptians to take shelter in the houses and not to stand in the fields or open places, lest they and their cattle die. Some were afraid and took shelter, but whoever did not believe and remained outside his house died in this plague. Here the mercy of the One who does not desire the destruction of the Egyptians, but their faith and repentance, is shown.

9.9.1.en: God's commandments are warnings to you, that you may repent before the day of judgment comes; likewise the guidance of your father of confession and all the teachings of the Church try to rescue you, so seize these opportunities to repent and set your way right, and even to establish a relationship with God so that you may enjoy His love.

9.10.0.en: Moses stretched out his hand, and the violent seventh plague began, consisting of three parts that combined together to destroy the wicked:

9.10.1.en: 1- Thunders: disturbing sounds that represent the warnings of God.

9.10.2.en: 2- Hail: sharp ice, which signifies the divine wrath from heaven.

9.10.3.en: 3- Fire: it burns whoever meets it, and it signifies our just God, who is a consuming fire. The wonder appears here, which is the union of fire with ice in one plague, because ice needs cold in order to form and fire is a heat suited to the hot climate and melts everything that is frozen.

9.11.0.en: This plague had never happened before in Egypt, because it is distinguished by a mild climate in which thunder and hail are rare, while fire is utterly foreign to its weather conditions.

9.11.1.en: God allows adverse and strange circumstances in your life that perhaps may lead you to repentance, so when you lose some of your possessions or your dignity, know that God is calling you to return to Him.

9.12.0.en: The hail struck all the stubborn who did not enter their houses, they and their cattle, and they died, and it also ruined and destroyed the plants and trees.

9.13.0.en: Here too God's distinguishing of His people is shown, for this plague did not come upon them like the rest of the plagues.

9.13.1.en: Your faith in God protects you from many troubles, so do not be disturbed by God's punishment of the wicked, because you are safe within His hand.

9.14.0.en: Stay any longer: continue to dwell in Egypt.

9.14.1.en: Pharaoh was alarmed by this plague more than by all the previous plagues, and for the first time he declared that he was a sinner and that God was righteous, and he humbly begged Moses to take this plague away from him, and promised to let the people go to worship God.

9.14.2.en: Do not rush into promises and vows during your distress because of your need, and then retreat from them when the crisis is relieved.

9.15.0.en: Moses agreed to pray for the plague to be lifted, but by God's guidance, as a prophet who knew of the hardness of Pharaoh's heart and that he was a liar and deceiver in his promises and would not let the people go.

9.16.2.en: Wheat: the grain, that is, wheat.

9.16.3.en: Rie: legumes such as beans and lentils.

9.16.4.en: The plague of hail came in the spring, when the barley and the flax were ripe, and this plague destroyed them, while the wheat and the legumes were only small plants, so they were not harmed and their crop was not ruined.

9.17.0.en: When Moses prayed, the plague ceased and the rain, the hail and the fire stopped.

9.18.0.en: After the plague ceased, Pharaoh returned to the hardness of his heart and refused to let God's people go. The plagues of the locusts and the darkness.
